claims.text: A short-duration, low-temperature annealing treatment can simultaneously increase strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
The relevant initial microstructure contains a ductile FCC phase and a hard B2 or similar phase.
Low-temperature annealing can selectively recrystallize the ductile FCC phase.
The same annealing treatment can preserve the architecture of the hard phase.
An annealing window exists below the recrystallization threshold of the hard phase but above the threshold needed to recrystallize the ductile phase.
Selective recrystallization of the FCC phase produces grain refinement.
Selective recrystallization of the FCC phase optimizes strain hardening.
The hard phase remains continuous and effective in carrying load after the proposed treatment.
Refinement of the ductile phase increases its ability to accommodate deformation and therefore increases ductility.
Refinement of the ductile phase increases work hardening.
Preservation of hard-phase integrity improves load partitioning.
Improved load partitioning increases overall alloy strength.
The treatment is expected to increase yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to an as-cast or conventionally heat-treated baseline.
The treatment is expected to increase elongation to failure relative to an as-cast or conventionally heat-treated baseline.
The simultaneous improvement is expected under ambient-temperature mechanical loading.
Annealing above the optimal temperature or duration may recrystallize the hard phase and negate the benefits.
Annealing outside the optimal window may fail to refine the ductile phase adequately and negate the benefits.
